B: Hiya, lovely! I'm Ceri. Oh, look at you, all cosy.
A: Hi. I'm Lauren. Sorry, I'm in my hoodie, I've just got in from a late shift.
B: Don't apologise, I'm in mine and all! Where are you, then?
A: Basingstoke. Erm, Hampshire.
B: Pontypridd, South Wales, me. What's the shift work, if you don't mind me asking?
A: I'm a vet nurse. At a small practice, just small animals.
B: Oh, a vet nurse! See, I've got an old Staffie, Bwbach, he's thirteen now. He's on the settee behind me, you can probably see his big head. Snoring.
A: Oh, I can see him! He's lovely. Thirteen's a really good age for a Staffie.
B: He's got a lump on his side, and the vet says it's a fatty one and to keep an eye. But I'm forever poking it, you know, measuring it with my fingers like a lunatic.
A: No, that's actually what you should do. Lipomas are really common in older dogs. If it gets bigger quickly, or goes hard, or he starts licking it, then sort of get it looked at again. But honestly most of them are just fat.
B: Oh, that's made me feel better, that has. Thank you. Better than the vet, you are, he just says "keep an eye" and charges me forty quid.
A: Ha, sorry. We do say that a lot.
B: I'm training to be an OT, occupational therapist, so I'm on placement and all at the minute. I'm a mature student, forty-one. Everyone on my course is about your age.
A: That must be quite hard, doing placements and essays.
B: It's the essays. The placement I love, I'm good with people, twenty years hairdressing. But the writing, oh my God. I left school at sixteen thinking I was thick, and sometimes I sit there with an essay and that feeling comes right back, you know?
A: Yeah. I didn't do uni either. I did an apprenticeship. I sometimes wonder if I'd have managed it, erm, if that makes sense?
B: Course you would! You're a nurse, you do drug doses and that. That's maths under pressure. Don't let anyone tell you that's not clever. Sorry, am I mothering you? I do that with the girls on my course.
A: No, it's nice. Thank you.
B: What's the hardest part? For me it's the patients who won't let you help, the proud ones.
A: Erm, phoning owners with bad news. And euthanasias. I'm the one holding the dog usually. I still cry in the car after sometimes.
B: Oh, love. That's not weakness, mind. That's what makes you good at it. My dad had a stroke, and the ones who were brilliant with him were the ones who sort of felt it, you know?
A: Is he okay now?
B: He's doing tidy. Slower. What's your cat called? I saw a ginger thing in your photo.
A: Biscuit. He came in to be put to sleep and I just, erm, kept him. That was four years ago.
B: Stop it! That's the loveliest thing I've heard all week. Four years! So he wasn't even poorly then?
